title: USCIS Is Using AI to Adjudicate Cases. Here's What That Means for Your RFE

sections.heading: What's Actually Happening
paragraphs: USCIS has been incorporating AI tools into parts of its adjudication workflow, joining a broader trend across federal agencies toward AI-assisted processing. The specifics of how these tools are used in any individual case aren't fully public, but immigration practitioners handling EB-1A and EB-2 NIW petitions have reported a noticeable pattern: Requests for Evidence that are longer than they used to be, but less internally coherent, sometimes referencing evidence inconsistently or raising points that don't fully track with the specific petition being reviewed.

This doesn't mean every RFE now involves AI, or that AI-assisted review is inherently less accurate. It does mean that petitioners and their representatives are encountering RFEs with a different character than the more tightly focused requests common in the past, and it's worth understanding why before you're staring at one on a ninety-day deadline.

sections.heading: Why This Matters for How You Respond to an RFE
paragraphs: If you receive an RFE that feels unusually long, references points that seem tangential, or asks for clarification on something you thought your original filing already addressed clearly, that's increasingly common under current adjudication patterns, not necessarily a sign that your case is in unusually serious trouble. The right response isn't to panic at the length. It's to carefully identify each specific point being raised, even ones that seem redundant or oddly framed, and address each one directly and completely.

A scattered or inconsistent RFE is, if anything, more important to respond to with tight organization and clarity than a narrowly focused one, precisely because it's easier to accidentally miss or under-address one of several points buried in a longer, less coherent request.

sections.heading: Why This Matters Before You File, Too
paragraphs: If adjudication increasingly involves automated review at some stage, even as a supplementary tool alongside human officers, the practical takeaway is the same one that's mattered all along, just more so: clarity and internal consistency in your petition matter enormously. A petition where your cover letter, your evidence index, and your recommendation letters all tell a clearly aligned, consistent story is easier to evaluate accurately, whether the reviewer is a person, a tool, or some combination of both. A petition with internal inconsistencies, vague claims, or evidence that doesn't clearly map to the criterion it's meant to support is more likely to generate exactly the kind of scattered, over-broad RFE this trend describes.

sections.heading: What This Doesn't Change
paragraphs: The legal standards for EB-1A and EB-2 NIW haven't changed because of how USCIS processes petitions internally. AI-assisted review, to whatever extent it's being used, is a tool for managing volume and consistency, not a new legal test you need to satisfy. The fundamentals remain the same: specific, well-organized, internally consistent evidence that clearly satisfies the applicable legal standard.

sections.heading: The Practical Takeaway
paragraphs: Treat this less as a reason for alarm and more as reinforcement of something that was already true: build your petition to be unambiguous. Don't leave room for a reviewer, human or otherwise, to misread or misconnect your evidence. And if you do receive an unusually long or scattered RFE, resist the urge to write a similarly scattered response. Organize your reply point by point, address everything raised, and keep your response as tightly structured as the original petition should have been.

intro: Over the past year, USCIS has been expanding its use of artificial intelligence tools in how it processes and adjudicates immigration petitions, including in the employment-based categories. This isn't speculative. USCIS maintains a public inventory of its AI use cases through the Department of Homeland Security. What's less discussed is what this shift actually looks like from the petitioner's side, and immigration practitioners have started noticing a pattern worth understanding.

faqs.question: Can I find out whether AI was used to review my specific case?
faqs.answer: Not directly. USCIS doesn't disclose which tools were involved in adjudicating an individual petition, though its general AI use case inventory is publicly available through DHS.

faqs.question: Does AI-assisted adjudication mean my case is less likely to be approved?
faqs.answer: There's no evidence that AI involvement itself lowers approval likelihood. The main practical impact practitioners have observed is in the character of RFEs, not in overall outcomes.

faqs.question: Should I change how I write my petition because of this trend?
faqs.answer: The core advice doesn't really change: be specific, be internally consistent, and make sure every claim is clearly supported by the evidence right next to it. That standard serves you well regardless of who, or what, is reviewing your case.

title: Is EB-2 NIW Actually Recovering? What the Approval Rate Rebound Really Means

sections.heading: The Numbers, in Context
paragraphs: USCIS approval rates for EB-2 NIW petitions dropped to a low point around the end of Fiscal Year 2025, then climbed for three straight quarters afterward. That's a real, measurable rebound. It's also still meaningfully below where approval rates sat a few years earlier, when EB-2 NIW approvals were running dramatically higher than they are today.

The honest takeaway is that the category isn't in freefall anymore, but it also hasn't returned to the more permissive adjudication environment of a few years ago. Treat any specific percentage you see cited, including the ones in this post, as a quarterly snapshot rather than a fixed number, since these figures shift and should be checked against current USCIS data before you build expectations around them.

sections.heading: What's Actually Driving the Rebound
paragraphs: The recovery doesn't appear to reflect a loosening of the underlying legal standard. The Dhanasar three-prong test hasn't changed. What's more likely driving the improvement is that petitioners, and the attorneys and consultants helping them, have adapted to what USCIS started demanding more rigorously back in late 2024 and early 2025: a specifically defined proposed endeavor, evidence with quantifiable, measurable impact, and clear alignment across all three Dhanasar prongs, rather than broad assertions of significance.
In other words, the rebound likely reflects better-prepared petitions meeting a standard that's still genuinely higher than it used to be, not USCIS relaxing its expectations.

sections.heading: What This Means If You're Preparing to File
paragraphs: Don't read the rebound as a green light to file the way petitions were built three or four years ago. The petitions succeeding in this recovering environment share specific traits: a narrowly defined endeavor rather than a general career description, quantifiable evidence of impact rather than descriptive language, and a coherent throughline connecting all three prongs rather than treating them as separate boxes to check.

If your current draft leans on broad claims about your field's importance rather than specific, measurable evidence tied to your particular endeavor, the rebound in approval rates doesn't protect you from that weakness. The cases still getting denied tend to share exactly that gap.

sections.heading: What This Means If You Already Have a Pending Case
paragraphs: If your petition was filed under the older, looser standard and is still pending, this is worth watching but not panicking over. Some petitions filed with a more general endeavor description are still succeeding, particularly where the underlying evidence is genuinely strong. If you're concerned about how your pending case reads against current standards, that's worth a specific review rather than general reassurance either way.

sections.heading: The Takeaway
paragraphs: EB-2 NIW is neither collapsing nor returning to its most permissive era. It's stabilizing at a higher evidentiary bar than a few years ago, with approval rates recovering as more petitioners meet that bar. The safest strategy right now is the same one that's been true through the entire shift: build a specific, quantifiable, coherent case, rather than betting on the trend line doing the work for you.

intro: For much of the past two years, EB-2 NIW approval rates have been the subject of a lot of anxious conversation, and for good reason. Approval rates fell sharply through 2025, hitting a low point in the final quarter of that fiscal year. Since then, quarterly USCIS data has shown three consecutive increases. The question worth asking isn't just "are the numbers going up," but "why, and does that actually change anything about how you should build your case."

faqs.question: Does the approval rate rebound mean EB-2 NIW is "easy" again?
faqs.answer: No. It's recovering from a particularly difficult period, not returning to the historically high approval rates seen a few years ago. The underlying evidentiary bar remains meaningfully higher than it was then.

faqs.question: Why did approval rates drop so sharply in the first place?
faqs.answer: USCIS sharpened its evidentiary expectations starting in late 2024 and early 2025, particularly around demonstrating measurable, quantifiable national importance rather than accepting broad assertions of significance.

faqs.question: Should I wait to file until the trend improves further?
faqs.answer: Generally no. The trend reflects better-prepared petitions meeting a stable, higher standard, not a temporary dip you can wait out. A well-built case filed today has a reasonable basis for approval regardless of which direction the quarterly percentage is moving.

title: EB-1A vs EB-2 NIW: How to Choose the Right Pathway for Your Profile

sections.heading: The Core Difference
paragraphs: EB-1A asks whether you, as a person, have extraordinary ability, meaning sustained national or international acclaim that places you among the small percentage who have risen to the top of your field. The evaluation is about your standing and reputation, measured against ten regulatory criteria.

EB-2 NIW asks a narrower, more specific question: does your proposed endeavor, meaning the particular work you plan to continue, have substantial merit and national importance, are you well positioned to carry it out, and would waiving the job offer requirement benefit the US. The evaluation is about your endeavor and your fit for it, not about your acclaim as a person.
Put simply, EB-1A is about who you are in your field. EB-2 NIW is about what you're proposing to do and whether you're the right person to do it.

sections.heading: When EB-1A Tends to Fit
paragraphs: EB-1A tends to fit people who already have external, verifiable markers of recognition: media coverage of your work, a documented pattern of being consulted or judged by others in your field, awards, or a leading role at organizations with strong reputations in their industry. If your career has already generated evidence that other people, not just you, consider your standing significant, EB-1A is often the stronger fit.

sections.heading: When EB-2 NIW Tends to Fit
paragraphs: EB-2 NIW tends to fit people whose individual acclaim might not yet meet the EB-1A bar, but whose specific work has clear, demonstrable importance. This is common among researchers early in an otherwise strong career, engineers and technologists solving problems with real national relevance, and founders whose ventures address a specific, significant gap. The case isn't built on "I am extraordinary." It's built on "this specific endeavor matters, and I'm positioned to advance it."

sections.heading: What If You're Genuinely Not Sure
paragraphs: Most people land somewhere in the middle on a first look, and that's normal. A few honest questions can help clarify it. Do you have independent, verifiable recognition of your standing, awards, press, judging roles, from people outside your own organization, or is your strongest evidence mostly internal to your work? Can you point to a specific, well-defined endeavor with measurable national importance, or is your case really an argument about your career in general? Would a stranger reading only your evidence, not your own account of it, conclude you're at the top of your field, or conclude your specific work matters at a national scale?
Your honest answers to those questions point toward one pathway more clearly than the category names alone ever will.

sections.heading: It's Not Always One or the Other
paragraphs: Some profiles genuinely support a case for either pathway, and in those situations, the decision often comes down to which case can be built more convincingly with the evidence currently available, not which category sounds more prestigious. A well built EB-2 NIW case beats a thin EB-1A case every time an adjudicator has to decide.

sections.heading: Making the Call
paragraphs: Choosing between EB-1A and EB-2 NIW isn't about picking the "better" category. It's about matching your actual evidence to the question that evidence answers well. Getting this decision right at the start saves significant time, since building toward the wrong standard for months before realizing it doesn't fit is one of the more expensive mistakes in this process.
If you're weighing both and want an honest read on which one your profile actually supports, that's exactly what a strategy session is for.

intro: This is probably the single most common question we get in a first strategy session, and it usually comes from people who assume the answer is about which category sounds more impressive. It isn't. EB-1A and EB-2 NIW ask fundamentally different questions, and the right pathway depends on which question your evidence actually answers well.

faqs.question: Can I file for both EB-1A and EB-2 NIW at the same time?
faqs.answer: It's possible to file separate I-140 petitions under different categories, though most people focus resources on building the strongest single case rather than splitting effort across two.

faqs.question: If I start with one pathway, does switching mean starting over?
faqs.answer: Some evidence carries over, since strong publications, letters, and documentation are usually relevant to either pathway. The strategy and framing, however, do need to be rebuilt around the different legal standard.

faqs.question: Does one pathway have a shorter overall timeline than the other?
faqs.answer: Not inherently. Timelines depend more on your country of birth, service center, and whether you use premium processing than on which category you choose.

title: EB-1A's Big Shift: From Discretionary to Non-Discretionary Review

sections.heading: What Changed
paragraphs: In 2025, USCIS issued Policy Manual guidance directing officers to apply a more objective, structured analysis when adjudicating EB-1A petitions, particularly at the final merits determination stage. The update reinforced that the EB-1A evaluation is not meant to function as a broadly discretionary decision, and instead directed officers to focus specifically on whether each regulatory requirement is satisfied by the evidence presented.

This is a meaningful shift in emphasis. Historically, final merits determination has involved a degree of officer judgment about whether a petitioner's overall record demonstrates the required sustained acclaim, judgment that could vary somewhat between officers reviewing similar evidence. The updated guidance pushes adjudication toward a more consistent, criterion-by-criterion analysis of whether the evidence actually meets the legal standard, rather than a broader, more subjective impression.

sections.heading: Why This Doesn't Mean EB-1A Got Easier
paragraphs: It would be a mistake to read "less discretionary" as "less demanding." The legal standard itself, sustained national or international acclaim placing you among the small percentage who have risen to the top of your field, hasn't moved. What's changed is that officers are being directed to check that standard more rigorously against the specific evidence in front of them, rather than making a more holistic, and potentially more forgiving, judgment call.

In practice, this tends to reward petitions with well-documented, specific evidence that clearly and unambiguously satisfies each criterion being claimed, and tends to penalize petitions that relied on a persuasive overall narrative without equally strong evidence behind every individual piece.

Some practitioners have also noted that despite this directive, a degree of officer judgment still shows up in practice at the final merits stage, particularly around how officers weigh evidence that technically satisfies a criterion but is borderline in strength. The shift toward objectivity is real, but it hasn't fully eliminated variation in how individual cases get evaluated.

sections.heading: What This Means for How You Build Your Case
paragraphs: Under this more structured review approach, ambiguity works against you more than it used to. If a piece of evidence arguably satisfies a criterion but requires some interpretation or benefit of the doubt to get there, that evidence is now more exposed than it would have been under a more holistically discretionary review. The stronger move is building your case around evidence that clearly, unambiguously satisfies each criterion you're claiming, with as little room for interpretation as possible.

This also raises the value of explicit, direct framing in your petition. Don't make an adjudicator connect the dots between your evidence and the legal standard on their own. Walk them through it explicitly, criterion by criterion, so the objective analysis they're directed to apply has an easy, clear path to a favorable conclusion.

sections.heading: The Bigger Trend
paragraphs: This shift toward a more structured, objective standard mirrors similar moves USCIS has made across other high-skilled immigration categories in recent years: less reliance on a case's overall persuasive quality, more emphasis on whether specific, documented evidence meets specific, stated requirements. Petitioners who treat their case as a legal argument that needs to be proven point by point tend to fare better in this environment than those who treat it as a compelling story that needs to be told well.

intro: A policy update most prospective EB-1A petitioners have never heard of has quietly reshaped how these cases get decided. It didn't change the ten regulatory criteria. It didn't change the final merits determination as a concept. What it changed is how much room an individual officer has to apply their own judgment when deciding whether your case clears that bar, and that distinction matters more than it might first appear.

faqs.question: Does this policy update apply to petitions already filed before it took effect?
faqs.answer: Generally, USCIS applies current policy guidance to petitions pending at the time of adjudication, regardless of when they were originally filed, so this standard likely applies to many petitions that were drafted before the update.

faqs.question: Does a more objective standard mean EB-1A approval rates have gone up?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. A more structured, criterion-by-criterion review can cut both ways, rewarding well-documented evidence while more consistently catching evidence that doesn't clearly satisfy a criterion, regardless of how persuasive the overall narrative sounds.

faqs.question: How is this different from the final merits determination that's always existed?
faqs.answer: Final merits determination as a legal concept hasn't changed. What's changed is the degree of officer discretion involved in applying it, with current guidance pushing toward a more consistent, evidence-focused analysis rather than a broader subjective judgment.

title: EB-1A vs. EB-2 NIW: The Approval Rate Gap Is Real, and It's Not Closing

sections.heading: The Numbers
paragraphs: Recent quarterly USCIS data has shown EB-1A approval rates running in the mid-to-upper 60% range, while EB-2 NIW approval rates have been more volatile, dropping into the mid-30% range at their lowest point before climbing back into the 50% range in more recent quarters. Even accounting for that recovery, EB-1A has generally maintained a higher approval rate than EB-2 NIW across this same period. As always, treat specific percentages as quarterly snapshots rather than fixed numbers, and verify current figures before relying on them.

sections.heading: Why the Gap Exists
paragraphs: The gap isn't primarily about one pathway being inherently more generous than the other. It's about self-selection and evidentiary structure.

EB-1A has an unusually high entry bar: sustained national or international acclaim, evaluated against ten specific, well-established regulatory criteria that have existed largely unchanged since the 1990s. Petitioners who file EB-1A cases tend to do so because they already have unusually strong, well-documented achievements, awards, media coverage, high-profile roles, that clearly satisfy defined criteria. The evidentiary bar to attempt EB-1A is high enough that weaker cases are more likely to be filtered out before filing, whether by the petitioner's own honest self-assessment or by an advisor's guidance.

EB-2 NIW, by contrast, has a comparatively lower baseline threshold to attempt: an advanced degree or exceptional ability, plus a case built around the three-prong Dhanasar test rather than ten specific, itemized criteria. That lower entry threshold means a wider range of profiles attempt EB-2 NIW petitions, including many where the proposed endeavor and its national importance are genuinely harder to establish clearly, which naturally produces more variability, and more denials, in outcomes.

sections.heading: What This Means for Choosing Your Pathway
paragraphs: The approval rate gap is not, on its own, a reason to prefer EB-1A over EB-2 NIW if your profile doesn't actually fit the EB-1A standard. Filing an EB-1A petition without genuinely sustained, well-documented acclaim doesn't inherit EB-1A's higher approval rate. It inherits a mismatch between your evidence and a demanding standard, which tends to produce a denial regardless of which category's overall statistics look better on paper.

The more useful question isn't "which category approves more petitions." It's "which category's specific legal standard does my actual evidence most convincingly satisfy." A well-built EB-2 NIW case, with a specific, well-evidenced endeavor and a clear throughline across all three Dhanasar prongs, has a stronger basis for approval than a thin EB-1A case that technically checks three criteria without genuinely demonstrating sustained acclaim.

sections.heading: The Real Takeaway From the Data
paragraphs: If anything, the approval rate gap reinforces something already true of both pathways: preparation and fit matter more than the category's overall statistics. EB-1A's higher approval rate largely reflects that EB-1A petitioners tend to file only when their evidence is already unusually strong. EB-2 NIW's more variable rate reflects a wider range of profiles attempting a standard that, done well, is entirely achievable, and done poorly, is not.
Choosing your pathway based on which one has a friendlier headline statistic, rather than which one your actual evidence supports, is one of the more common strategic mistakes we see in this space.

intro: Anyone comparing EB-1A and EB-2 NIW purely on approval statistics will notice a consistent pattern: EB-1A has been running meaningfully higher than EB-2 NIW in recent quarterly data. That gap is real, but reading it as "EB-1A is simply easier" misses what's actually driving the difference, and could lead you toward the wrong pathway for your specific profile.

faqs.question: If EB-1A has a higher approval rate, should I try that first even if I'm not sure I qualify?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. EB-1A's approval rate reflects that most filers already meet a high bar before filing. Attempting EB-1A without genuinely strong, well-documented evidence of sustained acclaim doesn't borrow that category's favorable statistics.

faqs.question: Does a lower EB-2 NIW approval rate mean the Dhanasar standard has gotten unreasonably strict?
faqs.answer: It reflects a combination of a genuinely higher evidentiary bar than a few years ago and a wide range of profiles, some stronger fits than others, attempting the category. A well-matched, well-evidenced case still has a solid basis for approval.

faqs.question: Can my profile realistically qualify for both categories?
faqs.answer: Some profiles do support a case under either pathway. In those situations, the decision typically comes down to which case can be built more convincingly with your specific available evidence, not which category's overall approval rate looks better.

title: The EB-2 NIW Backlog Nobody's Talking About, and What Exactly is Going On

sections.heading: The Scale of It
paragraphs: By the end of Fiscal Year 2025, more than 74,000 EB-2 NIW cases were sitting in USCIS's pending queue. That number reflects a category that's become dramatically more popular over the past several years. Filing volume grew sharply between 2020 and 2023, as awareness of the NIW pathway spread, particularly among researchers, entrepreneurs, and technical professionals looking for a route to permanent residency that doesn't depend on an employer sponsor. That growth in filing volume hasn't slowed down. Well over 66,000 EB-2 NIW petitions were filed in Fiscal Year 2025 alone, and that pace has continued into the current fiscal year.
Standard processing times have stretched to around 24 months for many cases as a direct consequence.

sections.heading: Why This Matters More Than It Sounds Like It Should
paragraphs: It's easy to treat "processing is slower" as a minor inconvenience. In practice, a growing structural backlog changes the calculus around several real decisions. If you're weighing EB-2 NIW against another pathway partly based on speed, the backlog means EB-2 NIW's timeline advantage over some alternatives has narrowed. If your current visa status has a hard expiration date, a 24-month or longer wait changes how much runway you actually need to plan for before you can even reach the adjustment of status or consular processing stage.

It's also worth understanding that a growing backlog isn't evidence that EB-2 NIW is becoming less viable as a pathway. It's evidence that more people are choosing it, which is a different problem with different implications for your own strategy.

sections.heading: Does the Backlog Affect Whether You'll Be Approved?
paragraphs: Not directly. Backlog size is a volume and capacity issue, not a merits issue. USCIS still adjudicates each petition against the same three-prong Dhanasar standard regardless of how many other cases are waiting in line. What the backlog does affect is how long you'll wait for that adjudication to happen, not how it will ultimately be decided.

That said, a longer pending period does mean your petition sits in the queue for longer, and circumstances can change during that window, in your field, your evidence, or your own career, that are worth keeping documented and current in case they become relevant to your case later.

sections.heading: What You Can Do Given a Longer Wait
paragraphs: Premium processing remains the most direct lever available for controlling your own timeline, since it guarantees a decision within its stated window regardless of the overall backlog size. It comes at an additional cost, currently a few thousand dollars, but for petitioners whose plans depend on timing certainty, it can be worth that cost specifically because it insulates you from the broader queue.

Beyond that, the most useful thing you can do is build the strongest, most complete petition possible from the outset, since a case that avoids a Request for Evidence effectively avoids adding months onto an already lengthy process. In a backlogged system, an RFE doesn't just cost you the time to respond. It often means going back into a queue that's continued growing while you were preparing your response.

sections.heading: The Bigger Picture
paragraphs: A larger backlog reflects a genuinely popular pathway experiencing real strain, not a pathway in decline. If anything, rising filing volume suggests more people continue to see EB-2 NIW as a viable route to permanent residency, even as processing times stretch out. Planning around a realistic, longer timeline, rather than the faster timelines common a few years ago, is simply part of building an accurate strategy today.

intro: Most conversations about EB-2 NIW right now focus on approval rates: are they up, are they down, what does USCIS want to see. Fewer people are talking about a quieter but equally consequential trend: the sheer number of pending cases has grown substantially, and that backlog is shaping processing times as much as any policy shift is.

faqs.question: Is the EB-2 NIW backlog expected to improve any time soon?
faqs.answer: There's no clear indication of when processing times will shorten, given that filing volume has continued growing rather than leveling off. Petitioners should plan around current timelines rather than anticipated improvements.

faqs.question: Does a longer pending period mean my case is more likely to receive extra scrutiny?
faqs.answer: Not inherently. Time in the queue reflects volume and capacity, not the depth of review your specific case will eventually receive.

faqs.question: Is it worth paying for premium processing just to avoid the backlog?
faqs.answer: For petitioners with a specific timeline need, a status expiration, a job transition, a personal deadline, premium processing can be genuinely worth the additional cost, since it removes your case from the general queue's uncertainty. For petitioners without a pressing timeline, it's a personal cost-benefit decision rather than a necessity.

title: Common Mistakes That Weaken EB-1A and EB-2 NIW Petitions

sections.heading: Treating the Criteria as a Checklist, Not a Narrative
paragraphs: In EB-1A cases especially, it's tempting to aim purely at satisfying three of the ten regulatory criteria and stop there. But three criteria satisfied with unrelated, scattered evidence tell a weaker story than three criteria satisfied with evidence that reinforces one clear, specific claim about your standing in your field. USCIS evaluates the whole record at final merits, not just whether individual boxes are checked.

sections.heading: Describing a Job Title Instead of a Proposed Endeavor
paragraphs: This is the most common flaw in EB-2 NIW petitions right now. A proposed endeavor needs to be a specific, well-defined body of work with its own evidence of feasibility and progress, not a description of your general occupation or career path. "Improving cybersecurity for financial institutions" as a general career description is vague. A specific method, applied to a specific problem, with evidence of its impact, is an endeavor.

sections.heading: Asserting Significance Instead of Demonstrating It
paragraphs: "My work has had a major impact on my field" is an assertion. It's not evidence. Adjudicators are increasingly looking for something measurable behind claims like this: citation counts, adoption by others, patents, documented outcomes, or independent recognition. A petition full of confident adjectives and thin on quantifiable specifics is more exposed than it used to be.

sections.heading: Recommendation Letters That All Sound the Same
paragraphs: When every letter in a petition shares the same structure and language, it stops reading as five independent confirmations and starts reading as one narrative repeated five times. This is one of the most avoidable weaknesses in a petition, and one of the most common, because it usually comes from giving recommenders too much of a template to work from rather than guiding them toward their own specific, independent account.

sections.heading: Relying Entirely on Evidence From Your Own Organization
paragraphs: A case built almost entirely on your own employer's internal reports, your own account of your significance, and letters from people who work closely with you can look self-referential, even when everything in it is true. Independent corroboration, from people, institutions, or publications outside your immediate circle, carries more weight precisely because it isn't self-interested.

sections.heading: Overreaching on Every Point
paragraphs: A petition that claims extraordinary significance for every single achievement tends to undercut its own credibility. Not every accomplishment needs to carry the same weight. Reserving your strongest claims for your genuinely strongest evidence, and describing everything else more modestly, reads as more credible, not less impressive.

sections.heading: Skipping the Underlying Eligibility Check
paragraphs: In EB-2 NIW cases specifically, it's easy to jump straight into building the Dhanasar argument without first confirming, explicitly, that the base EB-2 classification, an advanced degree, the bachelor's-plus-experience alternative, or exceptional ability, is clearly established. USCIS is checking this step more closely than it used to, and skipping it invites exactly the kind of RFE that could have been avoided.

sections.heading: Building the Case Alone, Too Late
paragraphs: None of these mistakes come from a lack of ability or achievement. They come from building the case itself without enough distance from your own work to see where the gaps are. Getting a second, more objective read on your strategy before you file, rather than after an RFE flags the problem, is usually the difference between fixing these issues cheaply and fixing them under a ninety-day deadline.
If any of these sound familiar in your own draft, that's worth addressing before you submit, not after.

intro: Most weak petitions aren't weak because the underlying achievements aren't strong enough. They're weak because of how the case around those achievements gets built. Here are the mistakes we see most often, across both EB-1A and EB-2 NIW cases.

faqs.question: Is any single one of these mistakes automatically fatal to a case?
faqs.answer: Rarely on its own. It's usually the combination, several of these weaknesses compounding across the same petition, that turns a strong profile into a denied or heavily RFE'd case.

faqs.question: Can these mistakes be fixed after I've already filed?
faqs.answer: Some can, particularly through an RFE response. Others are harder to fully correct after filing, which is why catching them beforehand is significantly less costly than catching them afterward.

faqs.question: Which of these mistakes is the most common?
faqs.answer: Describing a job title or general career path instead of a specific proposed endeavor is currently the single most common issue we see, particularly in EB-2 NIW cases.

title: What Makes a Strong Recommendation Letter for Your Petition

sections.heading: Why Letters Matter So Much
paragraphs: A recommendation letter is one of the only pieces of evidence in your petition that comes from someone other than you. Everything else, your cover letter, your CV, your evidence index, is your own account of your own significance. A letter is where an independent voice, ideally someone with real standing in your field, confirms that account in their own words.
That independence is exactly what makes letters valuable, and exactly what gets undermined when a petition's letters all read like they came from the same source.

sections.heading: The Biggest Mistake: Letters That Sound Identical
paragraphs: If five recommendation letters share the same structure, the same phrasing, and the same handful of adjectives, an adjudicator doesn't read that as five independent confirmations. They read it as one narrative, restated five times, which raises exactly the question you don't want raised: did these people actually write this, in their own judgment, or were they handed something to sign.
This is one of the fastest ways to weaken an otherwise strong petition, and it's almost always avoidable with more deliberate planning before the letters are drafted.

sections.heading: What a Strong Letter Actually Includes
paragraphs: A specific, personal basis for the letter. A strong letter opens by establishing exactly how the writer knows your work, not generically ("I have known the applicant for several years") but specifically ("I supervised the applicant's work on X project between 2021 and 2023" or "I reviewed the applicant's research as an editor at Y journal").

Concrete, verifiable detail, not just praise. "The applicant's contribution was significant" says nothing an adjudicator can check. "The applicant's diagnostic protocol reduced average time to diagnosis in our department by a measurable margin, and has since been adopted by two other departments" says something specific, checkable, and genuinely persuasive.

A distinct voice and structure from every other letter in the petition. Different recommenders should emphasize different aspects of your work, use different structures, and sound like different people, because they are. This isn't just a stylistic preference. It's what makes a set of letters credible as independent testimony rather than a template.

No shared phrases with your own petition documents. If a sentence in a recommendation letter closely echoes language from your cover letter or CV, it undermines the appearance of independence, even if the overlap was accidental.

sections.heading: Who Should Write One
paragraphs: The strongest recommenders are people with real standing in your field who can speak to specific, verifiable interactions with your work, not simply people willing to sign something flattering. A letter from someone with genuine authority in your field, who writes specifically and independently, is worth more than three generic letters from people with impressive titles but no direct connection to the work in question.

sections.heading: Getting the Process Right
paragraphs: Strong letters usually require some structured input from you, since your recommenders often need reminders of specific dates, projects, and outcomes you shared with them years ago. What they shouldn't need is a draft written in your voice for them to sign. The goal is guided specificity, not authorship.
If you're not sure whether your current set of letters reads as genuinely independent or as five versions of the same narrative, that's worth a second look before you submit them.

intro: Recommendation letters carry more weight in EB-1A and EB-2 NIW petitions than almost any other piece of evidence, and they're also the piece most petitioners get wrong first. Not because the recommenders lack standing, but because the letters themselves are often built the same flawed way: generic, interchangeable, and short on anything an adjudicator can actually verify.

faqs.question: How many recommendation letters do I actually need?
faqs.answer: There's no fixed legal number. What matters more than quantity is that each letter is specific, independently voiced, and genuinely corroborates a different angle of your case.

faqs.question: Can a family member write a recommendation letter?
faqs.answer: Family members generally lack the independent, arms-length standing that makes a recommendation letter persuasive. Letters from colleagues, supervisors, or others with direct professional knowledge of your work carry significantly more weight.

faqs.question: What if my recommenders are slow to respond or hard to reach?
faqs.answer: Give them a clear, specific request early, with enough lead time before your filing deadline, and be ready to send a polite follow-up. Building in extra time for this step usually prevents it from becoming a bottleneck.

title: Understanding Possible RFE Risks Under The Recently Updated USCIS Policies

sections.heading: Why RFEs Have Increased
paragraphs: The legal standards for EB-1A and EB-2 NIW haven't changed. What's changed is how closely adjudicators are checking whether petitions actually meet those standards with specific, verifiable evidence, rather than general assertions of significance. Petitions that would have passed on the strength of confident language a few years ago are more likely to draw a request for something concrete today.
That shift shows up most clearly in a handful of recurring RFE triggers.

sections.heading: The Most Common RFE Triggers Right Now
paragraphs: A vague or overly broad proposed endeavor. This is the single biggest driver of RFEs in EB-2 NIW cases. If your endeavor reads more like a job description or a general career direction than a specific body of work with defined scope, expect USCIS to ask you to narrow and clarify it.

National importance asserted, not demonstrated. Statements like "this work benefits the US economy" or "this research matters to public health" without a specific, measurable connection to that claim are a frequent RFE trigger. Adjudicators are increasingly looking for quantifiable evidence: adoption numbers, citation impact, patents, institutional partnerships, or documented outcomes.

Recommendation letters that all sound the same. When every letter in a petition uses similar language, similar structure, or repeats the same specific phrases, it reads as templated rather than genuine, and it invites questions about whether the letters reflect the writers' independent judgment.

Weak evidence for the "well positioned" prong in NIW cases. Simply holding relevant credentials isn't the same as demonstrating you're specifically positioned to carry out your proposed endeavor. USCIS is asking more often for evidence of a track record: past projects, resources, partnerships, or progress already made toward the endeavor.

Failing to establish the base EB-2 classification before addressing NIW at all. A surprising number of RFEs in EB-2 NIW cases start with USCIS questioning whether the applicant actually meets the underlying EB-2 requirements, an advanced degree, the bachelor's-plus-experience alternative, or exceptional ability, before even reaching the Dhanasar analysis.

sections.heading: How to Reduce RFE Risk Before You File
paragraphs: The most effective RFE prevention happens before submission, not after.

Define your endeavor narrowly enough to prove it, rather than broadly enough to sound impressive. A specific, well-evidenced endeavor beats an ambitious, vague one every time an adjudicator has to make a decision.

Back every claim of significance with something measurable. If you can't currently point to a number, an adoption pattern, or an independent source confirming impact, that's a gap worth closing before you file, not after USCIS asks about it.

Give your recommendation letters room to sound like different people, because they are different people. Distinct structures, distinct emphases, and distinct language make a set of letters more credible, not less thorough.
Confirm your base EB-2 eligibility explicitly in your petition, rather than assuming it will be taken for granted.

sections.heading: If You've Already Received an RFE
paragraphs: An RFE is a specific, documented list of what USCIS needs to see more of. That's actually useful information: it tells you exactly where your original filing fell short, rather than leaving you guessing. A strong RFE response usually means more than adding a stronger cover letter. It often means rebuilding part of the underlying evidence or reframing the endeavor itself, not just restating the original argument more forcefully.
Cases that arrive after an RFE are not lost causes. Some of the strongest outcomes we've seen start exactly there, once the case is rebuilt around what the RFE actually revealed.

sections.heading: Where to Go From Here
paragraphs: Reducing RFE risk isn't about writing more persuasively. It's about making sure your evidence answers the specific questions USCIS is actually asking right now, before you submit, rather than after.
If you're preparing to file, or already sitting with an RFE deadline, it's worth having someone look at exactly where your case stands against these current patterns.

intro: A Request for Evidence isn't the end of your case, but it's rarely a good sign either. It means USCIS looked at what you submitted and found it wasn't enough to decide, on at least one point, either way. Under current adjudication patterns, RFEs are landing on a more specific, more predictable set of issues than they used to, which means they're also more preventable than they used to be.

faqs.question: How long do I have to respond to an RFE?
faqs.answer: USCIS specifies a deadline directly in the RFE notice, commonly around 30 to 90 days depending on the type of request. Always confirm the exact deadline stated in your own notice rather than assuming a standard timeframe.

faqs.question: Can I request an extension on an RFE deadline?
faqs.answer: Generally, no. RFE deadlines are typically firm, which makes early, organized preparation of your response more important than trying to negotiate more time later.

faqs.question: Does receiving an RFE mean my case will be denied?
faqs.answer: No. An RFE means USCIS needs more evidence on a specific point before deciding. Many petitions that receive an RFE are ultimately approved once the response directly addresses what was requested.
